searchText: <@433705373070000138> 1559 is the simplest mechanism for fee burning that I know of, so even if the only goal was to burn fees, it would likely look like 1559. > <@!433705373070000138> 1559 is the simplest mechanism for fee burning that I know of, so even if the only goal was to burn fees, it would likely look like 1559. <@!301186049323958275> Well the simplist one, just burn all the fees is a terrible idea, so there is that. I mean, it wouldn't actually work. 🙂 But yeah, I suppose it *would* be the simplest solution. It would just result in 0 transactions. 😉 yeah, so lets not do that. I echo the sentiment that 1559 is pretty optimal for deciding how much of the fee to burn. And actually pretty simple. Congestion gets burned. Quick question Should we add an opcode to make BASEFEE observable? I'm leaning strongly toward yes by default There's a lot of value in an in-protocol gasprice oracle I feel like we almost need a beacon chain level for 1559 at this point with various versions. On one hand, there are a ton of good ideas that are being discussed and we'll definitely want to incorporate some of them in the final version, but on the other, using "vanilla 1559" will speed development up greatly for now, and probably still uncover some bugs. I'm not sure what's the best way to do this, but I'd be in favor of a sort of "spec freeze" (aside from bug fixes obviously) with what we have now (incl. the transition period, different tx types, etc.) and then in 1-2 months once we have more data about how 1559 is working, the various potential ideas and the outputs of some of the R&D work, we can do a major upgrade to a "v2". Curious what others think of this, and what the best way to do such a thing would be 🤔 I'm against a "spec freeze" for a few reasons: 1. I don't want to end up going to market with something that is sub par because we decided it was "too hard" to iterate. 2. I think iteration is critical in getting this right, which means getting things out there and testing them. 3. The engineering involved in 1559 is (IMO, engineer but not a client dev) not the long pole/bottleneck. 4. I think it is unlikely we'll see particularly interesting/useful data from integration testnets just because they don't represent the real world well enough. Any useful insights we can likely get from private single-client testnets which should be able to iterate pretty easily/freely and can target whatever they want (no need to coordinate). 5. Once we figure out that we want to do X instead of Y, it *feels* like a waste of effort to continue working towards X. For example, if a new client wants to add support for 1559 and join the integration testnet, they will have to first implement code that everyone knows is going to be dropped only to then excise that code later. In the case of the current open changeset, that means writing complicated code (migration code) that will be deleted when we drop the migration code (assuming the proposal gets general agreement and merged, which so far is looking likely). https://discordapp.com/channels/595666850260713488/749160974506000444/750046501639815200 > Yeah I think the idea was a minimum magnitude to the increment, whether it is in the positive or negative direction <@!376568077950910466> I am pretty sure (please correct me if I'm missing something) that we only need to set a minimum change on the way *up*, but not on the way down. I don't believe there is any value where we can get "stuck" such that we cannot go down anymore when we also *do* want to be able to go down? Yeah that's probably a misunderstanding on my part We may (need to think harder and it is late) get stuck on 1 and unable to go down to 0, but that seems acceptable to me. Desirable even? Actually, I wonder (but am too tired to find the answer right now), do we even need the `max` in there? If you cannot decrement from 2 to 1, then we don't need to worry about being able to increment from 1 to 2. Is it true for all cases that we necessarily can get out of any number we can get into? Might be worth the `max` just so we don't have to think about the answer to that question. 😬 That's a really good point, I also need to think on that. The issues I had with the parent baseFee being == 0 in the unit tests were because we set it to 0, not because it arrived there naturally. I need to check with the Besu team if that's true for their testnet tests where the issue arised. I'm pretty bad at mental math 😩 I think the "math is hard" and "max is cheap" is a compelling enough reason to keep it even if we *do* prove that it is unreachable. One of those things that just makes it so much easier to reason about. <@456226577798135808> Did you mean to make that comment over here? 🙂 Yes, sorry, got confused a bit 🙂 I agree that the spec should be only frozen when everything works in the implementation 🙂 because in this case, the spec isn't actually that large > I'm against a "spec freeze" for a few reasons: > 1. I don't want to end up going to market with something that is sub par because we decided it was "too hard" to iterate. <@!301186049323958275> No one was suggesting this. > 2. I think iteration is critical in getting this right, which means getting things out there and testing them. Okay, we all agree. > 3. The engineering involved in 1559 is (IMO, engineer but not a client dev) not the long pole/bottleneck. I think we all agree on this too. > 4. I think it is unlikely we'll see particularly interesting/useful data from integration testnets just because they don't represent the real world well enough. Any useful insights we can likely get from private single-client testnets which should be able to iterate pretty easily/freely and can target whatever they want (no need to coordinate). This is weird argument, regardless of if you find the results "interesting" this testing must be done, i'm not even understanding your point here, your next commment to Ian is on a bug that was discovered during integration testing... We already have a testnet running, it's already uncovering bugs, we can add some of the changes that have come up here. But I was never in favor of this nonsense development process, but it seem to be the only one that gets people to respond, so it's what we are sticking with. I don't know how a bunch of people who individually would never end up doing this stuff, collectively end up doing silly stuff, but that's like... you know... all of human history so... we should finish the testnet work that is going on now and suggest a bunch of patches for the next testnet. Yeah, I think maybe my "spec freeze" idea was too radical, but IMO we should have some pace around major iterations to the implementations -> QA (testnets) -> major iterations -> QA, etc. Especially given that we only have one implementation right now, I definitely think that spec-freezing right at the time when we discovered how to make the whole thing 2x simpler (getting rid of the two tx types) is a bad move But I do agree we need progress; pushing hard on a useful testnet after we finish that simplification is important

I feel like we almost need a beacon chain level for 1559 at this point with various versions. On one hand, there are a ton of good ideas that are being discussed and we'll definitely want to incorporate some of them in the final version, but on the other, using "vanilla 1559" will speed development up greatly for now, and probably still uncover some bugs. 

I'm not sure what's the best way to do this, but I'd be in favor of a sort of "spec freeze" (aside from bug fixes obviously) with what we have now (incl. the transition period, different tx types, etc.) and then in 1-2 months once we have more data about how 1559 is working, the various potential ideas and the outputs of some of the R&D work, we can do a major upgrade to a "v2". Curious what others think of this, and what the best way to do such a thing would be 🤔

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content:
I'm against a "spec freeze" for a few reasons:
1. I don't want to end up going to market with something that is sub par because we decided it was "too hard" to iterate.
2. I think iteration is critical in getting this right, which means getting things out there and testing them.
3. The engineering involved in 1559 is (IMO, engineer but not a client dev) not the long pole/bottleneck.
4. I think it is unlikely we'll see particularly interesting/useful data from integration testnets just because they don't represent the real world well enough.  Any useful insights we can likely get from private single-client testnets which should be able to iterate pretty easily/freely and can target whatever they want (no need to coordinate).

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: 5. Once we figure out that we want to do X instead of Y, it *feels* like a waste of effort to continue working towards X.  For example, if a new client wants to add support for 1559 and join the integration testnet, they will have to first implement code that everyone knows is going to be dropped only to then excise that code later.  In the case of the current open changeset, that means writing complicated code (migration code) that will be deleted when we drop the migration code (assuming the proposal gets general agreement and merged, which so far is looking likely).
